scenarios.title: My turn to defend the goal
scenarios.objective: Recognize the goal-defending turn and nearby crease.
scenarios.briefing: YOU have a short turn defending the navy goal at the -x end. The coach names the blue area in front of the net the crease. You are a skater taking a turn, not a permanent goalie. Gold1 has the puck; Navy2 takes the next turn. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: YOU are assigned the navy goal at the -x end.
The blue area is named the crease.
Navy2 is next in the rotation.

questions.prompt: Which goal are YOU defending?

options.text: The gold goal at the +x end
The navy goal at the -x end

questions.explanation: The briefing assigns YOU the navy goal at the -x end for this turn.

questions.prompt: What did the coach call the blue area by the net?
questions.explanation: The name is given in the briefing. This identifies an area, not a crease-entry rule.

questions.prompt: Arrange our goal-defending turns.
questions.explanation: This is the declared rotation; the coach controls the swap.

questions.prompt: Which facts belong to this activity?
questions.explanation: Gold1 owns the puck and Navy2 is next. The role is shared.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 gains control of the puck. Who has it then?
questions.explanation: The answer follows the stated change of possession.

questions.prompt: How could you help Navy2 enjoy the next turn?
questions.explanation: Encouragement and room to try are useful answers. No goaltending technique is scored.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 enters your support lane, what should you do?

options.text: Move to a new lane Navy2 can see

questions.explanation: Gold1 removed the first lane. A new visible lane can help the carrier without crowding the puck.

questions.prompt: What should YOU check after moving?
questions.explanation: The carrier and defender tell YOU whether the new support lane is useful. Empty ice alone is not enough.

questions.prompt: Place YOU below the carrier with space between you.
questions.explanation: This example gives Navy2 separation and another angle. A different clear support place may work.

questions.prompt: Why should teammates avoid sharing one small space?
questions.explanation: Two navy players in one spot can remove room and a passing lane. Separation lets Navy2 carry and see a target.

scenarios.title: A teammate behind your shoulder
scenarios.objective: Look beyond the forward direction to find a teammate.
scenarios.briefing: YOU face the attacking end and hold the puck. Navy2 is behind your facing direction. Gold1 is ahead on the other side. The coach asks you to find Navy2 before deciding on a puck action. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: Navy2 is behind that facing direction.
Finding Navy2 does not prove a pass is open.

questions.prompt: Where is Navy2 compared with the way YOU face?
questions.explanation: YOU face the attacking end while Navy2 is behind YOU.

questions.prompt: What can looking around help you find?
questions.explanation: Teammate locations and pressure are the source-supported information cues.

questions.prompt: Arrange this looking activity.

options.text: Tell the coach where Navy2 is

questions.explanation: This is the activity routine. A screen answer does not demonstrate a real shoulder check.

questions.prompt: For a second try, move YOU away from the side with Navy2.
questions.explanation: This changes the viewing relationship while leaving space. It is a practice reset, not an ideal game position.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 skates ahead of YOU. Should you keep pointing behind?
questions.explanation: Locate the teammate again when their position changes.

questions.prompt: Point to one thing you might miss by only watching the puck.
questions.explanation: Navy2 is a concrete example. A spoken answer or pointing is enough.

questions.prompt: Gold1 moves into the way ahead. What could YOU look for behind your shoulder?

options.text: Navy2 and a clear way to pass

questions.explanation: Navy2 is behind YOU. Looking there can reveal a different choice, but you still need a clear passing lane.

questions.prompt: What should YOU check before a pass back to Navy2?

options.text: Whether Gold1 can reach the passing lane
Only which way YOUR skates point

questions.explanation: A teammate behind you can help if you locate the target and check the lane. Facing forward does not remove the option of a pass back.

questions.prompt: Move Navy2 to a new waiting place behind YOU, with room for a short pass.
questions.explanation: Navy2 stays behind the way YOU face and separate from YOUR spot. Several nearby places can give a different passing angle.

questions.prompt: Why might a short pass back to Navy2 help you go forward later?
questions.explanation: It can move the puck away from Gold1’s pressure and give your team another view of the space ahead. Passing back is useful when that lane is clear; you do not have to use it every time.

scenarios.title: My partner has it now
scenarios.objective: Recognize the new puck owner after a completed partner pass.
scenarios.briefing: A gentle partner pass has finished. Navy2 controls the puck; YOU no longer do. This picture begins after reception and does not show the pass path. Leave Navy2 room while staying in the activity. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: The earlier pass is stated, not animated.

questions.prompt: Who controls the puck now?

questions.prompt: Does this picture show the whole moving pass?

questions.prompt: Put these stated events in order.
questions.explanation: This is the supplied history, not an independently simulated pass.

questions.prompt: Find separate space where Navy2 can still see YOU.
questions.explanation: This gives Navy2 room and leaves a visible partner. Other clear places may fit.

questions.prompt: Imagine Navy2 asks for a return target. What could you do?
questions.explanation: You can stay involved by getting available. A return pass still needs a clear route.

questions.prompt: What changed for YOU when the pass finished?
questions.explanation: YOU changed from having the puck to being without it. You can still help the activity.

questions.prompt: If Navy2 reaches the blue line first, what should you do?

options.text: Keep a clear space and find Navy2
Stand on the line without looking

questions.explanation: The named line is a meeting place, but Navy2's position and open space still matter. Arrive connected to the teammate.

questions.prompt: What two players matter near the meeting line?
questions.explanation: Navy2 is the teammate beyond the line and Gold1 is nearby pressure. Neither the line nor an unseen player decides the play.

questions.prompt: Place YOU closer to Navy2 while keeping Gold1 below you.
questions.explanation: This example moves YOU toward the teammate and away from the lower pressure. Another clear meeting spot can work.

questions.prompt: Why is the blue line a guide instead of the answer?
questions.explanation: It gives the activity a shared landmark. YOU still need to see Navy2, Gold1, and the open lane before carrying or passing.

scenarios.title: A mistake and another try
scenarios.objective: Respond kindly to a teammate error while noticing possession.
scenarios.briefing: In a friendly keep-away activity, Navy2 missed a pass and Gold1 gained the puck. The picture starts after that change. Navy2 looks to YOU for encouragement; the coach invites everyone to keep trying. Navy attacks the +x end; gold attacks the -x end. The full rink is an orientation map for this small activity.
cues: Everyone is invited to try again.

questions.prompt: Who has the puck after the missed pass?
questions.explanation: The current owner and stated event both identify Gold1.

questions.prompt: Which words could encourage Navy2?
questions.explanation: These are supportive examples. Other kind words may work too.

questions.prompt: Arrange one helpful response.
questions.explanation: This is a suggested routine, not the only acceptable order for showing support.

questions.prompt: For the next reset, find separate practice space near Navy2.
questions.explanation: This keeps YOU involved without occupying another player. It is a reset, not a defensive answer key.

questions.prompt: Imagine YOU miss the next pass. What could help?
questions.explanation: A mistake can lead to another supported attempt.

questions.prompt: Say one kind thing you would like a teammate to tell you.
questions.explanation: Any respectful encouraging answer is welcome. An adult can record the child's own words.

questions.prompt: If Gold1 controls the loose puck, what should navy players do first?

options.text: Read Gold1 and protect the navy end
Try a new touch after checking the puck

questions.explanation: Gold1 becoming the owner changes the role picture. Navy players should read the new carrier before choosing how to defend.

questions.prompt: What two clues shape the recovery after the miss?
questions.explanation: The puck state is loose and Gold1 is nearby pressure. The old pass did not complete, so it cannot guide the next touch.

questions.prompt: Place YOU beside the puck with Navy2 below you.
questions.explanation: This approaches the loose puck and keeps Navy2 in the support picture. Another controlled spot can work.

questions.prompt: What does “another try” mean after a missed pass?
questions.explanation: It means read the new loose puck, pressure, and support before trying again. Repeating the old pass without checking ignores Gold1's position.

scenarios.title: Find the loose puck and a friend
scenarios.objective: Find a loose puck, notice pressure, and choose a nearby teammate after the pickup.
scenarios.briefing: Navy attacks the +x end and gold attacks the -x end. YOU are skating toward a loose puck in open ice. Navy2 is across the middle with room. Gold1 is approaching from the side nearest the boards. The coach asks you to look while you approach, then choose what helps.
cues: The puck is loose in open ice.
Gold1 approaches from the board side.
